title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, and Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's baseline controls and operational procedures for: role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging standards, data residency and retention, Secure SDLC requirements, incident response (security-focused), compliance evidence workflows, and the process for risk acceptance and exceptions. It is intended for engineering managers, platform owners, security reviewers, and compliance stakeholders.

Scope

Applies to all Redwood-managed infrastructure, hosted controls, the Redwood control plane, customer-facing APIs, internal admin tools, and related developer workflows. Customer-specific private deployments may apply additional controls as documented in the customer's private-deployments runbook.

1) RBAC and Authentication Model

Principles
- Least privilege by default.
- Role-based permissions mapped to job functions (not individuals).
- Group > Role > Permission mapping enforced through identity provider (IdP) and provisioning pipelines.
- All elevated access requires just-in-time or time-bound elevation where possible.

Roles and High-level Permissions
| Role | Typical Members | Key Capabilities | Default Scope |
|------|-----------------|------------------|---------------|
| org-admin | SRE / Platform leads | Create orgs, billing, IAM delegation | Organization-wide |
| security-admin | Security engineers | Audit config, approve exceptions, view sensitive logs | Security scope |
| infra-engineer | Infra / Ops | Manage clusters, node pools, infra secrets | Project-level |
| service-account | CI/CD and internal services | Deploy, read/write runtime metrics | Resource-limited |
| developer | Product engineers | Deploy code, create non-sensitive routes | Project-level (no infra) |
| auditor | Compliance / Audit | Read-only access to logs and evidence artifacts | Organization-wide read-only |

Identity and Authentication
- Primary auth: SSO via the company IdP (OIDC/SAML). MFA enforced with platform policy (hardware token preferred).
- SCIM provisioning used for automated group membership sync from HR / GSuite / Okta.
- Service accounts are issued short-lived tokens (maximum 24 hours) and must be issued via the token service; long-lived secrets are prohibited unless approved via risk-exceptions process.
- Privileged sessions use just-in-time access (JIT) and are recorded; approval workflow is integrated with the access request system.

Access Review and Certification
- Quarterly access reviews for all high-privilege roles (org-admin, security-admin, infra-engineer).
- Automatic alerts for stale group membership (>90 days inactivity).
- Access revocation automation on offboarding (HR -> SCIM deprovisioning).

2) Audit Logging Standards

What we log
- Authentication events: successful/failed logins, MFA events, token issuance, token revocation.
- Authorization decisions: allow/deny for sensitive APIs, role changes, permission grants.
- Administrative actions: user creation/deletion, role assignments, policy changes, infrastructure changes that affect security posture.
- Data access events: read/write/delete of customer data, export/downloads, KMS operations.
- System events: deployment actions, configuration changes to production services, control plane changes.

Log Format and Integrity
- Canonical log format: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) including timestamp (ISO8601), actor, actor_id, actor_role, action, target, target_id, result, request_id, trace_id, and region.
- All audit logs are cryptographically signed at time of ingestion and stored with immutability markers (WORM) for retention periods subject to data residency rules.
- Example log entry:
{
  "timestamp": "2026-02-20T15:04:05Z",
  "actor": "alice@redwood.ai",
  "actor_id": "user-12345",
  "action": "role.assign",
  "target": "infra-cluster-prod",
  "result": "success",
  "request_id": "req-abcdef123"
}

Retention, Storage, and Access
- Audit logs retention defaults: 7 years for security-critical audit trails (compliant customers can request longer retention), 1 year for operational logs.
- Logs are partitioned by region and tenant; cross-region replication occurs only per customer residency policy.
- Storage backends: encrypted S3 buckets (or equivalent) with restricted bucket policies; bucket names and ARNs are recorded in the evidence inventory.
- Access to raw audit logs is limited to security-admins and auditors. Read-only access is provided to engineers via an audited query layer (e.g., Athena/BigQuery) that emits its own query audit logs.

Alerting and Monitoring
- Missing-log detection: heartbeat monitors detect ingestion gaps > 5 minutes and generate P1 alerts to the security oncall.
- Integrity alerts on signature failures or retroactive log rewrites trigger immediate investigation.

3) Data Residency and Retention

Data Classification
- Data classes: public, internal, confidential, regulated (PII/PHI/customer-sensitive). Each asset owner must classify datasets.

Residency Controls
- Customer data is stored in the customer-selected region by default (us-west-2, eu-west-1, etc.). Control-plane metadata may be stored globally but is pseudonymized for customer-sensitive identifiers.
- Cross-region replication only occurs after documented customer consent; replication must be logged as a data-access event.

Retention Policies
- Customer production data: retention configured per contract (default 90 days for transient runtime artifacts; customer-configurable for long-term storage).
- Audit logs: 7 years default for security-critical evidence; operational logs: 1 year.
- Backups: encrypted snapshots retained for 90 days by default. Longer retention requires approval and is added to evidence inventory.

Data Deletion and Legal Holds
- Data deletion requests flow through the Data Retention Service (DRS): request -> verification -> deletion job -> verification of deletion.
- Legal/Compliance holds suspend deletion and require a written request to compliance@redwood.ai. All holds are recorded in the evidence inventory.

Encryption and Key Management
- All data at rest is encrypted with KMS-managed keys. Customer-managed keys (CMKs) are available for Enterprise/Private deployments.
- Key rotation: CMKs rotated per customer policy; platform keys rotated at least annually. Keys are never exported; KMS audit logs are part of the evidence set.

4) Secure SDLC Requirements

Gates and Controls
- Threat modeling required for any design that handles regulated or customer-sensitive data or introduces new service-level permissions.
- Pre-merge checks: SAST, SCA (software composition analysis), and license checks are required.
- CI must run integration tests with test fixtures that exercise RBAC boundaries.
- PR review: at least one approver from the owning team and one security reviewer for security-impacting changes.

Release and Deployment
- Canary releases required for infra and runtime changes. Canary telemetry must be inspected for authorization-errors and elevated latencies for 24 hours before wide rollout.
- Deployment runbooks must include rollback steps and security verification steps (e.g., validate new logs are being emitted, validate IAM policies deployed as expected).

Dependency and Third-Party Policy
- Dependencies with known critical vulnerabilities must be remediated within 7 days or an approved risk exception must be submitted.
- All third-party services that process customer data must have a security questionnaire and SOC2/ISO attestation on file.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Detection and Triage
- Security detection playbooks define alert severity. P0/P1 security incidents escalate to the security oncall and the incident commander.
- Initial triage tasks: scope blast radius, identify impacted tenants, ingest related logs, collect in-memory artifacts if safe.

Containment and Eradication
- Containment options include isolating affected nodes, revoking service tokens, enabling emergency deny policies, and temporarily disabling affected endpoints.
- Eradication includes patching vulnerable components, rotating secrets and keys, and remediating misconfigurations. All remediation steps must be documented in the incident timeline.

Forensics and Evidence Preservation
- Preserve copies of raw logs, snapshots, and relevant KMS event records; write-once storage used for preserved artifacts.
- Forensic copies must maintain provenance metadata (who preserved, when, reason). Access to forensic artifacts is restricted and logged.

Communication and Regulatory Notification
- Communication templates exist for internal, customer, and regulatory notifications.
- Legal/regulatory notification thresholds (e.g., data breach involving PII) are mapped to notification timelines in the regulatory playbook. Compliance and Legal must be engaged within 24 hours of discovery for incidents meeting notification thresholds.

Post-incident Review
- Security postmortem must be produced within 7 business days for P0/P1 incidents and include root cause, timeline, mitigation, and action owners with deadlines.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Controls to Evidence Mapping
- Each control (RBAC, encryption, logging, SDLC, access reviews) maps to a canonical evidence artifact (policy document, access snapshot, log extracts, SCA report).

Evidence Inventory and Automation
- Evidence inventory is maintained in the compliance tracker. For each control we store: artifact_id, owner, retention period, and last-updated timestamp (automated where possible).
- Automations: daily snapshots of RBAC assignments, weekly exports of audit-log manifests, monthly dependency-scan reports.

Audit Response Playbook
- Pre-audit: compile evidence bundle 30 days before auditor start date.
- During audit: provide read-only access to auditors via an audited query layer, and share signed manifests for immutable artifacts.
- Post-audit: track findings in the compliance backlog and validate remediation within agreed SLA.

7) Risk and Exceptions Process

Exception Request Process
- Template required: risk description, impacted controls, compensating controls, risk owner, duration, and rollback plan.
- Submit via the security exceptions tracker. The request is reviewed by security-admins and the business owner.

Approval and Periodic Review
- Low-risk exceptions may be approved for up to 90 days. High-risk exceptions require a formal risk acceptance signed by a security leader and a business senior (VP++).
- All exceptions have a maximum duration of 12 months and are subject to quarterly re-review.

Compensating Controls
- Compensating controls must be measurable and monitored (e.g., additional logging, enhanced access reviews, network isolation rules).

8) Ownership, Contacts, and Escalation

Owners
- Security controls owner: Security (security@redwood.ai).
- RBAC policy owner: Platform IAM team (iam-platform@redwood.ai).
- Audit & evidence owner: Compliance (compliance@redwood.ai).

Escalation
- For missing logs or suspected tampering: immediate oncall escalation to Security Oncall -> Security Manager -> CISO.
- For suspected data-exfiltration affecting customers: Security Oncall -> Incident Commander -> Legal -> Customer Success.

Appendix A — Sample Commands and Queries

1. Querying audit logs (Athena / BigQuery style):
SELECT timestamp, actor, action, target, result FROM audit_logs
WHERE timestamp >= '2026-02-01T00:00:00Z' AND target = 'infra-cluster-prod'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC

2. Verify audit ingestion heartbeat (example curl against monitoring endpoint):
curl -sS https://monitoring.internal.redwood.ai/heartbeat/audit-ingest | jq
{
  "status": "ok",
  "last_event": "2026-02-20T15:02:45Z"
}

3. RBAC snapshot export (example CLI):
redwood iam export --org redwood --output rbac-snapshot-2026-02-20.json
